steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Atlanta GA. W-2 from Pacific Software: $68,200. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 3 clients), $2,650 from Barclays, $670 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 170 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,880/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2019–2021); $950 to Salvation Army have receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
I can walk you through this and give estimates and a clear checklist of what to do next. I’m not a tax professional, so treat this as general guidance — you may want to confirm with a CPA or tax preparer for filing.

Summary of the numbers you gave
- W-2 (Pacific Software): $68,200
- Freelance writing: $18,400
- Barclays: $2,650 (you said “from Barclays” — I’ll assume interest)
- Merrill Edge: $670 (assume interest/dividends)
- Total gross income: 68,200 + 18,400 + 2,650 + 670 = $89,920

Self-employment tax and business profit (estimate)
- Freelance net earnings depend on deductible business expenses. You listed $540 “unreimbursed expenses” — if these are business expenses for your freelance work, they are deductible on Schedule C. (If they are employee unreimbursed expenses, they are NOT deductible on your 2024 federal return.)
- Home office: 170 sq ft exclusive / 720 sq ft total = 170/720 ≈ 23.61% of the home.
  - Simplified method: $5 × 170 sq ft = $850 business deduction (no Form 8829 required).
  - Regular (actual) method: portion of rent attributable to business = 22,560 annual rent × 23.61% ≈ $5,323 (plus allocable utilities, insurance, etc.). You’d use Form 8829 for actual method.
- Example (using simplified home-office):
  - Schedule C net profit ≈ 18,400 − 540 − 850 = $17,010.
  - Self-employment tax: SE tax is ~15.3% of 92.35% of your self-employment gross. Using 18,400: SE tax ≈ 15.3% × (18,400 × 0.9235) ≈ $2,600.
  - You get an “above-the-line” deduction for half the SE tax ≈ $1,300.

Estimated AGI (rough, with simplified home-office)
- W-2 + Schedule C net + other interest = 68,200 + 17,010 + 2,650 + 670 = $88,530.
- Subtract half SE tax (~$1,300) → estimated AGI ≈ $87,230.

What you can likely deduct
- Charitable contributions: $950 to Salvation Army — deductible if you itemize (keep receipt). If you use standard deduction, you can’t separately deduct it on Form 1040 (unless special provisions apply).
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 deduction (adjustment to income) is available for qualifying loan interest. HOWEVER this phases out based on MAGI for single filers. With the AGI estimate above (~$87k), you are likely inside the phaseout range (so you may only get a partial deduction, or possibly none). Using the common 75k–90k phaseout range used in recent years, your allowed student‑loan interest deduction would be reduced (rough estimate: only a few hundred dollars allowed). Exact allowed amount depends on the official 2024 MAGI phaseout thresholds — I can compute a closer estimate if you confirm exact MAGI components and whether the Barclays/Merrill amounts are taxable interest/dividends.
- Home office:
  - Simplified method: $850 deduction (simple, often preferred when home-office allocation of rent/utilities is large relative to business income or for simplicity).
  - Regular method: you could claim ~$5,323 of rent as home-office expense (plus a share of utilities). That will reduce Schedule C profit more, but actual method requires Form 8829 and can only reduce the net profit to zero (cannot create a Schedule C loss attributable to home office beyond business profit limitations). If your Schedule C profit is small, the actual method’s larger deduction could be limited by business income.
- Business expenses: the $540 (if truly business expenses) is deductible on Schedule C.
- State/local taxes and property tax (SALT): you can include state income tax paid or state sales tax under itemized deductions, but there is a $10,000 SALT cap (if applicable). You did not provide GA state tax withheld or property tax — those matter for whether itemizing is worthwhile.
- Medical expenses, mortgage interest, etc.: not listed, so not included here.

Itemize vs standard deduction
- Standard deduction (single): generally larger than small itemized totals for many taxpayers. (For 2023 it was $13,850; it rises with inflation each year — confirm the 2024 standard deduction when filing.)
- Your known potential itemized deductions (charitable $950 + unknown state taxes) are probably less than the standard deduction unless you have sizable state tax, mortgage interest, or other itemizable amounts.
- Likely recommendation based on info given: take the standard deduction — you’d only itemize if your state tax + charitable + other itemizable items exceed the standard deduction. I can compare exact totals if you provide GA state tax withheld and any mortgage interest/property tax amounts.

Forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040 — main federal return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040), Part I/II — to report adjustments like student loan interest and other adjustments.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report your freelance writing income and business expenses (including home office if you use the simplified method you report the $850 on Schedule C; for actual method you attach Form 8829).
- Schedule SE — to compute self-employment tax.
- Form 8829 — only if you use the regular (actual expense) method for business use of your home.
- Schedule A — only if you choose to itemize.
- Schedule B — if you have more than $1,500 of taxable interest and/or ordinary dividends (your Barclays + Merrill amounts total $3,320 so you likely will need Schedule B if those are interest/dividends).
- Any 1099s you receive (1099-NEC for contract income, 1099-INT for interest, 1099-DIV, 1099-B for sales) — you must report these.
- Georgia state return (Form 500 or current GA form) — to report state income and compute any state refund/amount due.

Other points & recommendations
- Confirm whether the Barclays and Merrill amounts are interest, dividends, or something else (1099 interest vs 1099-B). That affects reporting (Schedule B vs Schedule D).
- Confirm whether the $540 unreimbursed expenses were business expenses for the freelance work. If yes, include them on Schedule C. If they are employee unreimbursed expenses, they are not allowed for federal itemized deductions (post‑TCJA rules).
- Decide home-office method:
  - Simplified ($5/sq ft) is easier and avoids Form 8829; if your actual rent allocation (~$5,323) is large but would be limited by business profit, simplified may still be cleaner.
  - If you choose the actual method, gather rent, utilities, insurance, and other home expense receipts for Form 8829.
- Because you have self-employment income, you owe self-employment tax (Schedule SE) and may owe additional income tax beyond withholding — you may need to make estimated quarterly payments for future years.
- Keep documentation: receipts for charitable gift, student loan interest statements (Form 1098-E if applicable), records of business expenses, 1099s.

If you want, I can:
- Recompute precise estimates if you give: GA state tax withheld (from W-2), confirmation whether Barclays/Merrill amounts are interest or dividends (and whether you received 1099s), and whether the $540 and the home office are strictly for the freelance work.
- Compare itemized total vs the standard deduction using exact 2024 standard deduction amount and your state taxes, mortgage interest (if any), and other itemizable amounts.
- Prepare a checklist of documents to gather for filing or for a tax preparer.

Which of the above would you like me to do next?
